scores.rationale: The strongest evidence comes from snippet [6] (Nisbet & Gurney 1989), which explicitly describes an intermediate range of low food levels where the animal 'neither dies of starvation nor resumes reproduction' — a direct theoretical statement of the stylized fact (while noting no data existed to test it). Snippet [5] similarly describes food levels too low for reproduction yet some individuals persisting. Snippet [13] shows reproduction continuing during weight loss/starvation, which mildly cuts against an absolute no-reproduction threshold but concerns decreasing rather than constant low food. Most other snippets are topically related (starvation, food thresholds, maintenance) but do not directly bear on whether a constant low-food regime permits survival yet never initiates reproduction. Overall the corpus offers moderate, consistent support with little genuine conflict, though much of it is theoretical/model-based rather than empirical.

scores.rationale: The stylized fact—that a range of constant low food levels permits survival but never triggers reproduction—is most directly supported by snippet [4], which explicitly models survival requiring a minimum consumption rate while reproduction requires a higher rate, implying a band where individuals survive but cannot reproduce. Snippets [1], [10], [16], [17], and [7] offer consistent but indirect support (low food limits/inhibits reproduction while maintenance/survival persists). The remaining snippets are merely topically related, addressing reproductive success variation, recruitment, or life-history trade-offs without bearing on the existence of a survive-but-no-reproduction food window. No snippet contradicts the fact. Overall there is moderate, mostly indirect support with one clearly aligned conceptual model and no conflict, so the direction is corroborative but evidence depth is limited.
